items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that some people can love Cirque shows and still not like Le Reve. But that comparison is really a separate discussion. To me the theater and visual design are the strong part of this show. The scenery and decor are breath taking from start to finish. The whole concept is really beautiful and appealing. Its just that it doesn't translate all that well to live performance. The storyline isn't that fun. When I went to see it once the stage broke down again and again all night. That made it hard to keep up with what was happening, even in the more impressive scenes. Le Reve seems to be reaching for some of the flair and spectacle that we associate with Cirque but it doesn't quite get there. I think I'll see it mainly for the beautiful theatre. Otherwise you might be better off putting your money towards another show.

So I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard, and I think I got about $38 worth of keyboard, maybe a little more. The space bar rattles, every thumb press gets a hollow clatter like a tray of cutlery being nudged. During the day I tune it out, but after midnight I find myself typing around it. The "E" key repeats now and then, so "meeting" becomes "meeeting". It happens once every few paragraphs, rare enough to forget about but frequent enough that I reread everything before hitting send.

I messaged the seller to ask what switches it used. Got tired of waiting, bought it anyway. Answer came a week later, after it was already on my desk. Brown switches, for the record.

The comfort is why I'm keeping it. Each key has a small bump partway down, so my fingers know a press registered without slamming to the bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists feel fine afterward, which the flat laptop keys never managed.

I did think about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of what I paid, and I'd be back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

I recently saw a theatrical circus production in Vegas and recommend it, but I'd give it one star less. The story is hard to follow, some songs just don't work, like one that made me sleepy, but the performers are great. Really good athletes. The women can be underwater for minutes at a time, that's wild.

The theatre is circular. The stage is circular. Every seat is a good seat. There are three main entrances. We see them being used throughout, they're more important during big scene changes. The stage and lighting and settings are really beautiful. It creates a real atmosphere, really memorable. And the tickets aren't too expensive. They're priced reasonably compared to other big Vegas shows, O or Love. I really wish there were more spectacular effects. More fire. Not a big deal. But it's a great show. It's really entertaining, really visually striking. Some of the music didn't work, storytelling wasn't easy to follow. But I recommend it.

Remote work gets talked about like it solves everything. Having mentored 5 junior engineers for about 2 years, I feel it is overblown, especially for juniors still learning how to code. Juniors don't really need the tickets or documentation or meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations, see how others debug, and ask questions before they've been confused for hours. This happens organically when you're in the office. With remote work they need to pick the right time to cut in, set up a call, explain a problem they might not even understand fully. That is a skill, and a tough one to have, before they get a chance to learn it.

I've seen the feedback problems with remote work. Short comments on code review feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. Also takes longer, so less momentum. My mentees typically improved faster with in-person pairing or whiteboard sessions, and easy access to seniors.

I don't want to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for juniors, proximity is a booster. It gives confidence, context, and instincts. If you just send a junior off with a laptop and a calendar, it can be a drag on their development, which could mean less good technical leadership down the line.

Its a bakery at 3:17 AM, the mixer is just humming, really loud, vibration goes through my boots. Its dark and flour dust is all over the air, catching the fluorescent light, looks like snow hanging there. The sourdough loaves are on wooden boards, still pale soft, not done with the final bake. I wipe my hands on the apron. Its stiff, dried dough and sweat. I move to the counter to check the lock. Its not needed really, just paranoid, a ritual.
There it was. The History of Salt, hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. Every Thursday for six weeks its been there, put exactly on the glass display case, next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp, and we are not a branch of the municipal system, so where does it come from. I picked it up, felt cold. I opened it and expected blank pages or some forgotten bookmark. Instead a square of lined notebook paper folded up slipped out, hit the counter, soft tap. I unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. It said, You knead with your left hand dominant, stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. I just stared at it. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. I look at my hands, red knuckled, dusted white. I closed the book. I put it back on the glass, aligned the spine perfectly with the edge. Then I turn off the overhead light above the display. Book is now in shadow.

The school we went to was Apple only. Middle and high school, just Apple. Cost like twice as much as the PC options. And the things broke down all the time, like once a month. Never dropped my laptop once but replaced the hard drive 5 times over 4 years, reinstalled OS many times. And then my friends MacBook Pro caught fire once while he was watching a movie. The smoke alarm went off. Apple support, they couldn't diagnose the issues, they just backed it up, wiped it, restored it. Same old story. Same with the iPhones. I had the very first one and it was always glitching. And now, they release a new iPhone every 2 months or so. A better camera, that's it. I'll grant you this, the iPads are the best tablets right now. But Android tablets will catch up in time.

I don't find it bad at all. I've been to Vegas constantly since I was a kid, so I've seen a ton of shows before I turned 21. Pretty good baseline. So the show itself, I just think it's very good. But not necessarily a Vegas must see. Would not make a trip for it. But I do think it's good, especially if you're staying at the Wynn or the Encore. The tickets are usually $125, but hotel guests can get them for $99. So if you're there, it's a good deal.

The circular stage is really clever. From just about every seat, you can see it. Which is pretty good. And the individual acts, I thought were impressive. The performers are very good, the aerialists and the acrobats, etc. But a lot of the things they do, I feel like I've seen them done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. So the problem is that the show is very hard to understand. The story isn't clear or really doesn't exist. I don't really know what the show was trying to say. But it's just very busy, very busy. Too many things going on at once, too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many "Wow" moments. If it was more restrained, I think it would have been better.

But aside from a few cool stunts, I thought it was just a pretty average show. I didn't feel blown away or anything. Nobody else felt blown away. A few people did enjoy it. If you haven't seen it, you should check it out. If you stay at the Wynn or the Encore, it's a good deal. But I wouldn't see it again, or pay full price to see it again. It's one of those shows that's trying to be a stereotypical Vegas show, where more is better. But more is just more.

Got a skateboard at Zumiez, went back for the rest of the kit. First impressions were good, me my friend and his little brother were chatting with a woman who was assembling the board. She was a manager, said she'd been putting together boards every day while working there. Said that on bad days she'd be annoyed and treat customers or other people badly. Assembly took 90 minutes, expected 15. She stripped two bolts then put them back in a way that suggested they'd be sold to another customer later. She got her brother and another employee who was also a manager to finish or help with it. No apology. Lost the future business. My heart is broken.

Bought this mechanical keyboard second hand for 38 dollars and it has been a chaotic but decent ride. The seller communication was terrible. I asked about the switch type before buying and they took a week to respond with one word. By then I had already taken the gamble and ordered it. The board is well loved. The spacebar rattles like a loose Lego brick which is incredibly annoying, and the E key sometimes repeats so I get typos like theee instead of the. But despite the quirks I really love typing on it. The tactile feedback is fantastic and its really comfortable for hammering out long painful work emails. I considered shipping it back but returning a 38 dollar heavy slab of plastic was more hassle than it was worth. So I kept it and honestly I have grown fond of its flaws. If you don't mind a little DIY tuning and the occasional double typed letter its a budget win.

Turkish airlines is such a nightmare. I was flying domestic Harbin to Beijing, then connecting to Istanbul. My Harbin flight was delayed and I missed the connection. Went to their booth and literally nobody wanted to help or take responsibility. Spent the night at the airport. Next morning asked for a ticket, and they told me all the flights were overbooked and I might be stuck for days unless I paid for business class. I needed to be in Istanbul so I paid. I am so mad and can't believe it.

So bring just one broken thing you need fixed, not two. When you get there, go get your number at registration, hold onto it, it goes in a queue. The repair people are volunteers, so it's first come first served. We can't promise we can fix everything, some things just won't work out. And pick your item up by 4pm or it's gone, we don't keep anything overnight, no exceptions. So make sure you have time to wait your turn, it can be long. Keep your number safe. That's it, hope it runs smoothly, thanks for going with it.

Its a float valve on the trough and a float that floats up when water comes in. When it drops, float drops, valve opens, lets water in. As it rises, float rises and valve closes. At the set level, valve shuts off. So why does it overflow? Two reasons, debris in the valve, calcium buildup or dirt gets in there, doesn't close fully, it just keeps trickling water in. The other reason, float is adjusted too high, so it closes after it's already overflowed.

So we went to this place Sunday night, showed up 7:20 because we had a 10pm show at the same hotel and thought it'd be easy. Never got to eat though so I can't even say if the food was good. They have this useless digital waitlist, we put our names in, they told us come back at 8:23pm to pay. We did, but then stood around until 8:40pm and then staff just casually mentioned probably won't be seated till 9:15. Just a party of two. They offered zero solutions, if the wait extends that far past payment just tell people upfront. So our night wasn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster, zero stars if it were an option.

Its one of those holiday seasons that are tough. Between everything going on inside Enron and everything going on outside. But I'm not sure if we should do the holiday party on the 8th. People have been talking about it. Some think its a good opportunity for all Enron employees to get together and celebrate. Some feel its not appropriate. I understand both perspectives. But after everything that's happened over the past month, we've decided to cancel the party. Spending money at this point on a celebration is something that could easily be seen as imprudent. And its a risk we shouldn't take. I'm sorry. You've worked hard and you deserve recognition. And a reason to celebrate. We'll look at other ways to recognize your contributions, ways more appropriate for the holiday season. Ken Lay

So a siphon moves water from one container to another, going over a barrier that is above the water level. Its gravity and air pressure are what push the water over and let the flow continue. The tube needs to be full of water first so the whole thing is one continuous column. Gravity pulls water down the longer leg that dips lower. That going down pulls the water out of the top of the siphon and drops the pressure there. Air pressure is pushing down on the source water, which forces more liquid up the shorter leg, filling that low pressure spot, and flow goes on. The outlet has to be lower than the source water surface. The pressure drop is the difference in weight of the water columns between the two legs. If the outlet is higher or level, gravity doesn't pull hard enough to lift water up the intake side. The net pull on gravity only exists when the coming out leg is heavier than the one going up. The air gets in the tube and it stops the siphon because it breaks the chain of water molecules that lets the suction effect travel through the tube. So the pressure equalizes with the outside air, no pressure difference and the flow stops. So the siphon is dead. Unless you fill the tube up again with water.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it again. Its always a Thursday, always on top of the flour bin, always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with a Richmond Public Library stamp on it. I never hear them come in past the squeaky screen door, but at 3am my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine so who knows. Tonight though a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron, left a white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. It said in really spiky handwriting, page 142. Please. I think they are watching the drop box now. A cold draft went through the kitchen, smelled like wet asphalt and coming rain. I looked at the front windows, just my own tired reflection in the dark. I did not open the book. Carefully tucked the note back between the pages, put the novel in a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it.

Paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard. I'd say it was $38 worth, maybe a bit more. First the flaws. The space bar rattles, not a gentle click but a hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it, like nudging a tray of cutlery. I stopped noticing during the day, but at night it sounds louder than it has any right to be. The E key occasionally repeats, so "meeting" becomes "meeeting". Happens about once every few paragraphs which is often enough to keep me proofreading. Communication with the seller was slow. I asked what switches it used before buying and the reply came a week later, after the keyboard had already arrived. Brown switches for the record. But the surprising part is it's genuinely comfortable. The keys have a satisfying cushioned feel and I can write long emails without my wrists complaining. That's more than I can say for the flat laptop keyboard I was using before. I did consider shipping it back but the hassle didn't seem worth it. So it stays on my desk, rattling and repeating and quietly earning its keep. Three stars.

unbiased rating: 4 stars. personal rating: 2.5 stars. i had never wanted to see cirque du soleil before, so le reve was my first show. i was expecting lots of backflips and extreme acrobatics but there was way less of that and way more interpretive dance than i anticipated. the performers are seriously good, undeniably, but its just not my style. anyone who really likes this kind of theatre will probably enjoy it. for me though, i wouldnt spend over $100 to see it. fortunately i got free tickets and im very glad i didn't pay.

Old school attendance registers are pretty useful for reconstructing daily life. Historians use them to figure out who was there and who wasn't and how often, and sometimes why they missed. This helps you infer things like seasonal work demands, illness, bad weather, poverty or family stuff, migration, local emergencies. So you can see patterns by gender, age, neighborhood, social class. And how education fitted into work and household routines and community expectations. Across many years, you get changes in schooling habits and public health. But the thing is the registers only record what the school chose to note. They don't really go into what the kids experienced. Absences get misreported or are incomplete and teachers might have their own assumptions. So they're really only useful when you compare them to other sources.

I think this person is a baker. She works at this bakery, and so every Thursday at 2:17 AM, this book will appear on the back step of the bakery. And it's always the same book, this field guide to North American moths, and it's from the county library. There's a ghost-pale sticker on the spine. The jacket has a little flour in it, as if the book was helping. She returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. On the third week, she just kept it by the rye starter, didn't say anything. Tonight it's raining, rain is ticking on the alley door. The ovens are breathing. Mara is making croissants, pushing the butter into the dough, and then the latch gives a little guilty click. Nobody's there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete. She wipes her hands on her apron and opens it. There's a slip of paper between Luna moth and Promethea, folded once. It says: your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. Sorry about the crumbs. Mara looks out at the alley, the dented milk crates, the steam coming off the drains. And the city is huge for a second, and then it isn't. She tears the corner of an order pad and writes, cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. And then she puts the note inside the book, sets it on the windowsill, and unlocks the back door.

So we did a classroom project where we compared how stable different folded cardboard bridge designs are. It was pretty simple, same cardboard each time, tried to keep length and width as consistent as possible. Short beam ones, arch-inspired, and triangular folds. Placed them between two supports and we just put weights on them slowly and watch them bend, tip or collapse. It was limited because we made them by hand, only small number of trials and it was in a classroom, so dont treat the results as proper engineering data. The triangular folds seemed to hold weight better and more steadily, so it does seem like fold geometry affects stability of these model bridges.

The book was sitting on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. Marguerite found it. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. It had a Harbor Street branch stamp inside, due date in March. The mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch beside it that the flour man used never latched properly. Eleven Thursdays she had asked the day staff and checked the hatch for scratches and once she stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four and she was always at the ovens, her back to the door when it did. Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers, ink gone blotchy where someone pressed too hard. I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. She smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it was because the pages did. Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt, bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. Tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

I live in Toronto now so I don't use Hydro Ottawa anymore, but I want to warn people about their billing practices, which are alarming. For about a year I had an account while renting a downtown apartment, and then I moved back in with my parents to do my MA. I formally cancelled it and paid up. But Hydro Ottawa kept taking money out of my bank account at random intervals for over a year, even after I cancelled it. I called customer service many times, sent proof of the withdrawals, and the reps said my account was closed and nothing was being charged. Turns out they'd linked my bank info to my parents' billing number by mistake because I'd mentioned moving back home. My parents didn't notice that they kept getting overpayment refunds, so the credits felt normal. It took hours on the phone and talking to a few different people before a manager looked into it. They confirmed the error and fixed it, but at first they said no refund and just gave an apology. That's insane. And my banking details are gone. So I won't ever use auto debit with them again. Their careless handling of your data really worries me.

3:40am. Second batch of rye still proofing, Marisol finds it again, the library book on the flour bin by the back door. Plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, due three weeks ago. Every time she carried it to the drop box on her way home. Every Thursday it comes back, like the building itself borrowed it. Wiped her hands on her apron, opened it. A folded index card slipped out from the barn owls page. "You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then, she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. —R." Marisol read it twice, oven timer counting down, the fan outside humming, pushing warm air into the dark. She turned the card over and with the grease pencil she uses for marking trays, wrote Rye's out at 4:15. Then she tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top, and propped the back door open just one inch.

I used to fly Ryanair as a broke student because my ex lived in Sweden and Ryanair was the cheapest way to get there. Honestly it was awful. At the airport they took my £20 L'Occitane shower gel, saying it was over the liquid limit but it wasn't. They said I could get it back if I went to the airport pharmacy and bought a 100ml bottle. So I did, came back, and they had no idea what I was talking about. Brilliant. £20 down the drain and I was livid. On top of that, they charged me £5 at the gate for having a bottle of water in my cabin bag, even though I'd bought it inside the airport.

They've since stopped flying Liverpool to Stockholm Skavsta, so I fly Norwegian now. Norwegian's customer service is also poor, funny how life works, but at least the planes are newer and not as decrepit as Ryanair's fleet.

You're not alone in this, it happens to everyone. I got absolutely hammered on Tuesday, and by Thursday half my Brandywines had let go. You can see the seam running right down the side of the fruit. Its the old story, dry spell then a sudden deluge. The inside of the fruit takes in water faster than the skin can stretch to keep up. The Sungolds are holding out mostly but I've got a few of them looking like they might follow.

You can't really get around weather once its happened, that thick skin the Brandywines have is a real liability in a storm like this. The only thing that helps a bit is keeping that two day schedule you've got on more of an even footing. Its not much help in the end though once the sky decides to let it all out at once. You'll likely get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use. You might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting quite so much water in a single go.

College Board has no limits to its hypocrisy. A friend of mine sat the SAT subject test, the 1 hour test, but the proctor messed up and gave the room about 20 extra minutes. My friend is very integrity oriented, and since she knew that this unfair advantage messed with the whole standardized test nature, she reported it through their official hotline. So as not to let this behavior continue. And the outcome? Pure institutional injustice. After an investigation they said there was insufficient evidence of misconduct to hold the proctor or the other students accountable. But very absurdly they said there was enough evidence of misconduct by my friend and they canceled her scores. They punished the honest person and let the actual violator off scott. This proves how unfair and broken this org is.

Thursdays it shows up. Not on the counter, no, its wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, like whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it. Its always the same one, *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, Elmwood Branch, due date stamped so long ago the ink has gone violet. I have never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow deep in rye dough by 2pm, and honestly at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band. First few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register, and by Friday morning its gone. Then Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I talk to my sourdough starter so I'm not judging.

Tonight there is a note tucked at page 114. The luna moths.

"They only live a week, they don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before its gone?"

No signature. Just pencil, pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.

So a room can feel stuffy even if the temp is fine. temp is just one factor. If humidity is high it slows the evaporation of moisture from your skin, makes it feel heavy and stale. And low air flow plays a part. without air moving, the c02 you breathe out, the odours, and heat just stays around your body. bad ventilation makes it all build up so it feels close and oppressive. So aircon will make it cooler but it won't necessarily reduce humidity or get air moving. Opening a window or putting a fan on or the ventilation system will help make it feel better by moving the air and reducing the moisture.

You get told remote work is a win for everybody. I've mentored five junior engineers for the last two years and it isn't. They don't need tickets, docs, or a set of scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else get through a nasty bug, and get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't get yet. That is a pretty steep thing to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment. And the lag on getting answers kills any forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. That's how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they are going to need. You are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

A rain gauge is a simple device, it just catches rain. It reports depth in millimetres or inches. That depth is the level water would be if it stayed on flat ground, so no drainage or evaporation, and nothing soaks in. Most gauges use a funnel with a wide opening, feeds into a narrow measuring tube. The same volume rises higher in the narrow tube, so small amounts are easier to read. The scale is marked to account for the area ratio so you still get true rainfall depth. Wind is a big source of error, gusts around the gauge can just blow rain past the opening and undercount. And then if it evaporates before you read it, or rain splashes around the gauge, that distorts results.

Bought this one used for 38. Pulled it out of the box and it looked fair honestly. A bit of dust between the keys, some shiny spots on the caps, but nothing worse than I expected from a second hand board. Good part is it is genuinely comfortable. I write long emails for work and my hands feel less cramped than on my flat office board. Switches have a steady feel, not too heavy, and the case doesn't slide around my desk. Problems: the space bar rattles every time I hit it, loud enough that I notice during quiet mornings. The e key occasionally repeats, so I get words like neeed if I type too fast. Doesn't happen constantly but happens enough that I proofread more carefully. Also asked the seller what switches it had. Answered a full week later, after the keyboard had already arrived. Not great. Still, for 38 I kept it. Shipping it back felt like more trouble than it was worth.

Just bring one broken thing per person. You have to check in at the front table and get a numbered ticket, keep it till your item gets back to you. Volunteers call numbers one by one. You should hang around because sometimes they need you there, or a decision. They can't fix everything. Parts to order or it's just not possible. When you leave the cafe, don't leave your item. After 4:30 PM, the volunteers leave and if you don't take it, you don't get it back.

went Friday around 4:30 pm to this buffet. Surprised there was no line. So I didn't have to wait. Two of us spent about $130 which is pretty steep. I thought it'd be comparable to a steakhouse but after actually learning more, it was somewhat more. So I was disappointed they didn't offer steak. That's the first thing I would look for at a buffet of this price. They did have lamb, prime rib, chicken. But those are things you can find at a lot of other Vegas buffets for a lot less. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are pretty common, I've been to a lot of buffets in Vegas that have them. But rock crab claws I haven't seen anywhere else, so those were interesting. But the problem was no crab crackers. The staff said we could get wooden mallets. But our table was right next to another table and I didn't want to start cracking shells and sending little pieces of shell over to the other people. So just ate the crab legs. The Asian station wasn't that distinctive, reminded me of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Desserts, they had gelato, pastries. Nothing really stood out. They did have fresh juices but I didn't try any of it. So overall I think it's acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. I think if you're curious, it's worth trying once. But if there's a long line, I'd reconsider.

Old school attendance registers are really valuable primary sources for historians. They try to reconstruct the rhythms of daily life in past communities. Meticulously tracking student presence lets them see patterns, like seasonal agricultural cycles, epidemics and bad weather. So a sudden drop in attendance might mean a flu outbreak or harvest time where kids had to work, showing the balance between education and work. Consistent absenteeism from certain groups could be pointing to social inequalities or cultural attitudes toward school. But you have to be careful. There is a big problem with these records. Teachers or headmasters might have fudged the numbers to get more funding or dodge scrutiny. So the data doesn't always tell you what actually happened. On top of that, registers don't explain why kids missed. Researchers are left guessing causes from other sources. And even though these logs give you numbers to look at community dynamics, you really need to cross-reference them with other historical evidence or you'll misread what was actually going on.

We have a float valve on the water troughs and it works like this. It's connected to a pressurized water line, just so you know. There's a float, it's just a plastic ball or block, and it sits on the water surface attached to the lever. So when the cows drink and the water level drops, the float sinks, it tilts the arm and that pulls the plunger or washer away from the valve seat. That's how water gets in. As the water goes up, the float lifts with it. The lever pushes the plunger back against the seat and gradually narrows the opening, and then flow stops at the set level. Overflow happens when the washer is worn or has debris on it and won't seal against the seat. Also when the float gets punctured and waterlogged so it doesn't rise enough to close the valve.
